title: Building work capacity with cardio specificity
summary: NH explains why bodybuilders need work capacity (cardiovascular stamina, ability to repeat efforts between sets, and recovery between sessions) and how to build it through set multiplication, higher training frequency and staple high-rep lower-body lifts. He argues cardio should be specific to your practice, done with weights via giant sets and circuits rather than treadmills or steppers.
claims: You should never have to end a set of squats or deadlifts because you are out of breath while the muscles still have reps left; fix it by slowing tempo or improving cardiovascular fitness
High muscular endurance lets you tax the baseline more and more over time, which leads to growth
Eventually the only way to add volume or frequency is to lengthen sessions, which requires work capacity
If you hit a weight for 6 reps and after 3 minutes rest can only get 3-4, that performance crash signals poor work capacity unless technique or context changed
Needing about 10 days before you can deadlift again means your recovery and work capacity are poor
Most people's training is too focused on intensity and not enough on repeating and multiplying sets
Instead of 2 sets of 3-6 squat reps, do 3-4 sets with slightly more reps and less weight to build work capacity
Lighter, higher-rep sets are less intense in absolute terms but can reach the same relative intensity
Evolving references let you cycle between very intense low-volume sessions (e.g. 1 set of 3, or 2 sets of 4 and 3) and higher-volume sessions (e.g. 6, 5, 4 reps) within a 1-3 sets of 3-6 scheme
Alternating intense and volume sessions in quick succession, outside of a block structure, is beneficial for bodybuilding
Set multiplication also happens across the week: train more often, because the only way to get better at recovering is to push the performance there
You may need to temporarily sacrifice low-rep references for higher reps and more sets, then return to low reps and see the improved capacity
Work capacity degrades again if you simply go back to low reps, so maintenance strategies are needed
Keep at least one squat or deadlift variation (knee flexion or hip hinge) as a permanent staple done for high reps, 6-12, never below 6
Lower-body lifts are best for building work capacity because they tax the whole body; overhead pressing rarely overtaxes you
Avoid pockets of time dedicated only to work capacity, like pseudo-deload weeks of light high-rep work; that tends to be junk volume
NH does all his cardio with weights: giant sets and high reps, never ellipticals or stair-steppers
Paused squats and Romanian deadlifts done often are building blocks for work capacity; RDLs do so without overtaxing strength work
Treadmills, jump rope and stair-steppers are orthodox bodybuilding cardio but neither specific nor necessary
Make cardio specific by identifying what in your program is most taxing on the cardiovascular system and making it easier over time, e.g. via variation, shorter rests or giant sets
Weight training is not very metabolically demanding because you can rest as long as you want, so you must actively seek out breathlessness
Example giant set: 10 reps of a lower-body movement, then a weighted carry, then an ab movement; you will be panting
Three sets of paused squats carry over far more to leg size and squat strength than 30 minutes on a treadmill
Weighted cardio has a recovery cost but saves time and works synergistically with the rest of training
End upper-body days with an endless giant set, e.g. push-ups, lateral raises and face pulls repeated until reps stop being quality
In giant sets with no rest you naturally slow the tempo and improve form because that is your only chance to catch your breath
Strongmen can do specific cardio with farmer's walks for distance or hiking; powerlifters with squats or rack pulls/isometric pulls, since bench rarely leaves you breathless
Cardio is boring but necessary for health and performance, so make it tolerable by doing something linked to your practice
exercises: pause at the bottom; do often for high reps
very challenging, builds work capacity and carries over to leg size
builds work capacity without overtaxing strength
Upper-body giant set (push-ups, lateral raises, face pulls)
no rest between movements; slow tempo; full external rotation on face pulls
Rack pull / isometric pull against pins
taxes metabolic system with possible strength carryover
